strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically important question: when and why Gaussian universality breaks down in high-dimensional ERM. The taxonomy distinguishing performance, score, and minimizer universality (Section 1.2, Table 1) is a genuinely useful contribution to an area where these notions are often conflated.

The main conceptual result—the decomposition of the test score as x^T θ̂ ≈ x^T μ* + α* z (Theorem 6.1)—is clean, interpretable, and yields a crisp characterization ('x^T θ̂ Gaussian iff x^T μ* Gaussian'), clarifying exactly where the Montanari & Saeed (2022)/Mallory et al. (2025) score-universality route fails.

The extension of CGMT to concentrated non-Gaussian column designs (Claim 4.1) with an explicit deterministic mean vector μ* is a natural and potentially valuable generalization; Remark 4.2 clearly explains why the mean/fluctuation split matters.

Theorem 7.1 (subspace confinement of μ*) is a nice structural result that makes the score-universality condition verifiable in structured models, and the equivalence with Mai & Liao (2025) (Appendix F) situates the work well in the literature.

The empirical evidence (Figure 1 elastic-loss experiment, Figure 2 MNIST, Figure 4 regularization sweep) directly illustrates both breakdown and validity regimes, and code availability is claimed. The paper is generally well-written and honest about scope (e.g., explicitly noting Lasso is excluded by Assumption 2).
weaknesses: The central result (Theorem 4.3) is not rigorously proven. The paper itself states that Claim 4.1—the non-Gaussian CGMT on which Theorem 4.3 rests—is 'still only a conjecture' (Section 4), and the abstract's claim that 'we derive an asymptotic min–max characterization' overstates what is established. Several proof steps are flagged as 'details omitted' (Proposition C.5's Lipschitz argument, stability of the saddle point in the proof of Theorem 4.3), which is not acceptable for a result positioned as the paper's core contribution.

The convergence of μ̂θ to μ* in Theorem 4.3 is argued by comparing argmins of E[Φ_μ(X)] and E[φ_μ(x,g)] at fixed μ; this requires uniform (in μ ∈ R^p) convergence of objectives, which is not established anywhere—the pointwise convergence from Claim 4.1 is insufficient for convergence of minimizers over an unbounded parameter space.

Assumption 4 (minimizer universality) is introduced as a standing assumption with a proof described as 'under preparation' (Section 6). Consequently, Theorem 6.1—the headline score characterization—is conditional on an unproven heuristic. This is honest, but it means the paper's two most quotable results are conjecture-dependent.

The main experiments use very small dimensions (p = 30, n = 50 in Figure 1), which weakens the support for asymptotic (p = Θ(n) → ∞) predictions; no study of convergence rates with growing n is provided.

The manuscript contains notational and labeling inconsistencies that undermine confidence: 'Proof of Proposition 7.1' corresponds to Theorem 7.1; the closed form of ξ_y in Appendix D.1 is attributed to '(14)' but appears as (15) in the main text; equation (44) drops the κ argument of ξ_y; several symbols (α_κ vs α) are used inconsistently in Appendix D.

Assumptions 2–3 (C^2/C^3 losses and regularizers, strongly convex ρ, bounded third derivative) exclude most practically interesting penalties (Lasso, group lasso) and non-smooth losses; while acknowledged, this narrows the scope considerably relative to the generality suggested by the abstract and Table 1.
The multiclass extension (Claim A.1) is explicitly conditional on 'Assuming the claim is also valid in these cases,' compounding the reliance on unverified claims.

Reproducibility: the code statement is truncated in the manuscript and no repository link is provided; the deterministic saddle-point problem (6) involves expectations over (x, y) that require numerical integration for general non-Gaussian designs, and details on how this is done are not given.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely important and timely question: precisely when Gaussian universality holds or breaks down in high-dimensional ERM. The distinction between performance, score, and minimizer universality (Section 1.2, Table 1) is a useful conceptual contribution that clarifies confusion in the literature.

The proposed deterministic characterization (Theorems 4.3/4.4) unifies fixed-point systems previously derived via RMT, AMP, and CGMT, and the explicit decomposition of the test score into a structured non-Gaussian component x⊤μ* plus an independent Gaussian fluctuation (Theorem 6.1) yields a clean and interpretable criterion: the score is Gaussian iff x⊤μ* is Gaussian.

The quadratic-surrogate result for smooth regularizers (Theorem 3.3) is a clean structural observation that simplifies the fixed-point analysis and is shown to be consistent with classical RMT results (Section 5, Appendix D).

The experiments are well chosen to illustrate the phenomenon: the bimodal/elastic-loss example (Figure 1) and the MNIST analysis (Figure 2, Appendix G) convincingly demonstrate that moment-matched Gaussian surrogates fail, and that the authors' non-Gaussian prediction tracks the empirical distribution while Gaussian-score-based predictions do not.

The paper is honest about the status of its results: the conjectural nature of the key CGMT extension (Claim 4.1) and the unproven minimizer universality assumption (Assumption 4) are explicitly disclosed, and code is said to be available.
weaknesses: The central technical claim is not rigorously established. The 'Generalized CGMT for concentrated column designs' (Claim 4.1) is explicitly labeled a conjecture ('which is still only a conjecture'), yet Theorem 4.3—the paper's main result—is presented as a theorem under Assumptions 1–3 and its proof simply invokes this claim. The abstract frames the work as a 'heuristic extension' of CGMT, but the body presents unconditional-looking theorems. This mismatch between the rigor claimed and the rigor delivered is the decisive weakness.

Several key proofs are incomplete. The proof of Proposition C.5 (concentration of α̃ and the bias bound |E[α̃]−α*| ≤ C/√n) contains 'details omitted' at precisely the two steps that would require real work (boundedness/Lipschitzness of α̃, and comparison of the expected shifted objective with the deterministic limit). The proof of Theorem 4.3 also defers 'stability of the saddle point (details omitted)'. The proof of Theorem 7.1 is terse and appears mislabeled ('Proof of Proposition 7.1'), with a decomposition argument whose orthogonality conventions need justification.

The score universality characterization (Theorem 6.1) relies on Assumption 4 (minimizer universality), which the authors acknowledge is unproven—a proof is merely 'under preparation.' Thus the paper's headline characterization of when Gaussian universality breaks down is itself conditional on an unverified heuristic, weakening the claimed clarification of the universality landscape.

Incremental novelty relative to prior work. The deterministic equivalent in Theorem 4.4 closely parallels fixed-point systems already in Montanari & Saeed (2022), Mai & Liao (2020/2025), and Pesce et al. (2023); indeed Appendix F shows the authors' equations are equivalent to those of Mai & Liao (2025) for LFMMs. The genuinely new content—the explicit role of μ* and the non-Gaussian design CGMT—rests on the unproven Claim 4.1.

The framework excludes the most practically relevant nonsmooth settings: Assumption 2 requires strictly convex, smooth losses and strongly convex regularizers, ruling out Lasso and nonsmooth losses that are standard in the CGMT literature. Combined with the concentration requirement (Assumption 1), the class of models covered is substantially narrower than the framing in the introduction suggests.

Theorem 3.3 is claimed to be 'equivalent to Theorem 4.3 presented below,' which creates an unclear logical dependency structure between the two headline results; if they are equivalent and one depends on a conjecture, the status of both needs to be stated more carefully.

Empirical validation is limited in scale (p = 30, n = 50 in Figure 1) and the MNIST experiment lacks important details (dimension, sample size, exact loss and regularizer, how the 'theoretical density' is computed without the conjectural claim being verified). Quantitative comparisons across multiple loss/data regimes would be needed to support the generality claims.

Presentation issues further reduce reliability: notation inconsistencies (e.g., C_θ̂ defined as E[θ̂θ̂⊤] − μθ̂μθ̂⊤, but later statements about tr(C_x C_θ̂) implicitly assume centering conventions; the class-conditional extension in Claim A.1 uses ∇ρ(μ*) with per-class α_ℓ in ways that are not carefully derived), and Theorem 7.1's regularizer ρ(θ) = a⊤θ + θ⊤Hθ omits the conventional 1/2 factor.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely question: when does Gaussian universality hold or break down in high-dimensional ERM? The explicit disentangling of three distinct notions (performance, score, and minimizer universality) is a genuine conceptual contribution and clarifies confusion present in the literature (e.g., the discussion of the 'unavoidable subset' condition of Montanari & Saeed 2022 / Mallory et al. 2025).

The decomposition of the estimator into a deterministic informative component mu* plus a Gaussian fluctuation of scale alpha* is an appealing and interpretable framework, and the resulting characterization (x^T theta_hat ~ x^T mu* + alpha* z; score Gaussian iff x^T mu* Gaussian) is a clean, useful statement.

The fixed-point system of Theorem 4.4 recovers known RMT/CGMT equations in special cases (ridge regression, LFMMs of Mai & Liao 2025, whose equivalence is derived in Appendix F), which supports the consistency of the framework.
The Table 1 comparison of assumptions and guarantees across the literature is informative and helps position the contribution.

The MNIST experiment (Appendix G, Figure 2) demonstrating simultaneous failure of score and performance universality on realistic data is a valuable empirical complement, and the code is reported to be available, aiding reproducibility.
The paper is transparent in places about the status of its results (e.g., explicitly flagging Claim 4.1 as a conjecture and Assumption 4 as unproven).
weaknesses: Soundness of the central contribution is not established. The 'generalized CGMT' (Claim 4.1), on which Theorem 4.3 — the paper's main theorem — rests, is explicitly described as 'still only a conjecture'. The abstract's claim of 'deriving an asymptotic min–max characterization' is therefore overstated: the derivation is heuristic, and Theorem 4.3, Theorem 4.4, Corollary 5.1, and downstream results are all conditional on an unproven claim.

Theorem 6.1 (asymptotic behavior of the test score), the paper's headline result on score universality, requires Assumption 4 (minimizer universality), for which the authors themselves state a proof is 'under preparation'. This is another major unverified pillar.

Several proofs contain substantial gaps or are incomplete: Proposition C.5's proof relies on '(details omitted)' claims (Lipschitz dependence of alpha-tilde on h, boundedness of Moreau derivatives); the proof of Theorem 4.3 invokes 'stability of the saddle point (details omitted)'. These are non-trivial steps, not routine verifications.

The proof of the subspace confinement result (Theorem 7.1 / 'Proposition 7.1' in Appendix F) appears flawed: the Jensen inequality argument yields E[e_L] >= e_L(E[x | x_I, y]^T mu* + alpha z), but E[x | x_I, y] equals x_I + E[x_N], which is not shown to equal x_I^T-direction in F + span(a); the step from conditional expectation to e_L(x^T mu_Fa + alpha z) silently assumes E[x_N] = 0 or that the projection of mu* is aligned, neither of which is justified. Additionally, the labeling switches between 'Theorem 7.1' and 'Proposition 7.1', and the rho(µ*) bound (51)-(53) drops cross terms without justification.

The assumption set is restrictive relative to the claimed generality: smooth, strongly convex regularizers exclude the Lasso (acknowledged); Assumption 1 (uniform concentration for all 1-Lipschitz functions of the full data) is strong; and Assumption 3's conditions on the third-derivative tensor rule out many natural penalties. The practical scope of the framework beyond Gaussian-like concentrated designs is unclear.

Experimental validation is thin: the synthetic experiments use very small dimensions (p=30, n=50) for results that are asymptotic in nature, and beyond the ridge case there is no systematic quantitative comparison of the theoretical predictions (e.g., no convergence studies across n). The MNIST analysis is illustrative rather than a rigorous test of the theory.

Presentation issues undermine confidence: Theorem 3.3 is said to be 'equivalent to Theorem 4.3 presented below' without explanation of in what sense; Section 6 contains the informal statement 'we are not aware of any empirical counterexamples' as a justification for an assumption; the roles of Corollary 7.2's moment conditions and Figure 4 are confusingly presented. There are also typographical/formatting glitches (e.g., equation (44) attributing a proximal expression to '(14)').

The novelty relative to existing work needs sharper delineation: the multiclass extension (Claim A.1) is itself admitted to rely on 'assuming the claim is also valid', and the reduction to Mai & Liao (2025) shows substantial overlap of the fixed-point equations with prior work, so the incremental technical advance beyond known results (mostly on the Gaussian and LFMM sides) is limited.

strengths: The paper makes a genuinely useful conceptual contribution by disentangling three inequivalent notions of 'Gaussian universality' (performance, score, minimizer) and providing a careful comparison table (Table 1) that situates its contributions against the RMT/AMP/CGMT literature. This taxonomy and the explicit identification of where universality breaks down are valuable for the community.

The authors are refreshingly honest about the conditional status of their results: the non-Gaussian CGMT extension is explicitly labeled a conjecture (Claim 4.1), and the dependency of each theorem on this conjecture and on Assumption 4 is clearly flagged.

The fixed-point system (Theorem 4.4) is shown to recover, as special cases, several rigorously established results (Karoui 2013; Bean et al. 2013; Dobriban & Wager 2018; Mai & Liao 2025 LFMM equations, worked out explicitly in Appendix F.1), which provides nontrivial indirect support for the conjectural framework.

The quantitative predictions are validated numerically in several settings (elastic-loss teacher–student model with bimodal features, ridge regression, MNIST), and the MNIST experiment (Appendix G, Figure 2) demonstrates both score-universality failure and the resulting performance-prediction failure on realistic data.

The covariance-adjusted subspace confinement result (Theorem 7.1) and the criterion 'score Gaussian ⟺ xᵀμ* Gaussian' are clean, interpretable structural statements that explain when and why moment-matched Gaussian surrogates fail.
Code availability is stated, and the written proofs provided (appendices B–F) are generally careful for the parts that do not depend on the conjecture (e.g., Theorem 2.1, Proposition 3.1, Lemma 3.2).
weaknesses: The central technical claim — the generalized CGMT for concentrated non-Gaussian column designs (Claim 4.1) — is an explicitly stated conjecture, not a theorem. Consequently the paper's flagship result (Theorem 4.3), the quadratic-universality result (Theorem 3.3, which is 'a consequence of ... Theorem 4.3'), the score characterization (Theorem 6.1), and the confinement result (Theorem 7.1, which builds on the conditional Theorems 4.3/4.4) are all conditional. The genuinely unconditional content is comparatively modest (concentration of θ̂ and the quadratic approximation of the regularizer).

Assumption 4 (minimizer universality) is itself unproven: the paper cites a proof 'under preparation' (Louart, 2026 — a preprint not yet available). Building a headline characterization of universality breakdown on a second unverified assumption further weakens the evidential chain.

The 'saddle-point stability conditions' invoked in the derivation of Theorem 4.3 (uniform τ-strong convexity of the profiled objective, O(n^{-1/2}) gradient sensitivity, local-uniform convergence to a unique stable minimizer, per Proposition C.5) are assumed rather than verified for the ERM application, so even the conditional chain has unverified links.

The assumption set is restrictive: twice continuously differentiable, strongly convex losses and regularizers (excluding the Lasso and other non-smooth penalties central to the CGMT literature), plus Poincaré-type concentration. Many of the settings in which universality breakdown is of practical interest fall outside this scope.

Novelty relative to recent work is somewhat limited: Mai & Liao (2025), Pesce et al. (2023), Hu & Lu (2022), and Mallory et al. (2025) already establish universality breakdown and CGMT extensions in overlapping settings; the main new element here is the (conjectural) unified framework rather than new provable phenomena. The difference in scope versus these works is documented but the marginal technical advance is conditional.

Simulation dimensions are small (e.g., p = 30, n = 50 in Figure 1), so the numerical evidence for an asymptotic (n → ∞) conjecture is suggestive rather than conclusive; no systematic finite-size scaling study is presented.

Minor presentation issues: a LaTeX artifact 'lambda2' appears in the covariance deterministic equivalent (Appendix D.3), and the conditional derivation of Theorem 4.3 leans on compact-truncation and uniform-integrability hypotheses 'stated in the main text' only informally, which hampers reproducibility of the argument.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely question: precisely when Gaussian universality holds and when it breaks down in high-dimensional ERM, and it usefully disentangles three often-conflated notions (performance, score, and minimizer universality) in Section 1.2 and Table 1, which is a genuine contribution to clarity in the literature.

The decomposition of the estimator into a deterministic mean µ* and fluctuation scale α* (Theorem 4.3) is an appealing and interpretable framework, and the covariance-adjusted subspace confinement result (Theorem 7.1) is a concrete, cleanly proven structural insight with an instructive Gaussian-mixture example.

The authors are admirably transparent about the conditional nature of the analysis: Claim 4.1 is explicitly labeled a conjecture, and Assumption 4 is flagged as unproven, rather than being presented as established theory.

The experimental evidence (elastic-loss experiment in Figure 1, ridge regression in Figure 3, MNIST in Appendix G) is well chosen: it demonstrates both regimes where universality holds (squared loss) and fails (η > 0, MNIST), and the theoretical predictions track the empirical score distributions in the non-Gaussian setting.

The recovery of prior fixed-point systems (Karoui/Bean/Donoho–Montanari, Dobriban–Wager, Mai–Liao LFMM in Appendix F.1) plus the RMT cross-check in Appendix D.2 shows the framework is consistent with, and extends, existing exact-asymptotics results.
weaknesses: The central technical device, the generalized CGMT for concentrated non-Gaussian designs (Claim 4.1), is a conjecture, not a theorem. The paper's headline results (Theorem 4.3, Theorem 3.3, Corollary 5.1) are all conditional on it, so the abstract's claim to 'derive an asymptotic min–max characterization' overstates what is actually established. No partial proof, special case, or error analysis of the conjecture is provided; the evidence is purely numerical.

Theorem 6.1, the paper's characterization of score universality ('x⊤θ̂ Gaussian ⟺ x⊤µ* Gaussian'), rests entirely on Assumption 4 (minimizer universality), whose proof is cited as 'under preparation' in a 2026 preprint (Louart, 2026) that is unverifiable and not available. A key claim of the paper thus depends on non-existent, non-archival evidence.

Several proofs defer crucial hypotheses rather than verifying them: the derivation of Theorem 4.3 invokes 'uniform-integrability and local-uniform concentration hypotheses' and 'saddle-point stability conditions' that are assumed but never checked, even in the concrete ridge example of Section 5 where they could plausibly be verified.

The unconditional, rigorously proven results (Theorem 2.1, Proposition 3.1, Lemma 3.2, Theorem 7.1) are supporting lemmas of a conditional program, not standalone contributions of independent value; Theorem 7.1 in particular only holds 'under Assumptions 2 and 3, let (µ*, α*, κ*, ν*) satisfy Theorem 4.4' — i.e., conditionally on the conjectured fixed-point system.

The validating simulations are small-scale (p = 30, n = 50 in Figure 1), far from the proportional asymptotic regime the theory targets; finite-size effects could mask inaccuracies of the conjectured comparison principle. No systematic scaling study (e.g., n up to thousands) is presented to confirm convergence to the predicted limits.

Scope restrictions are significant: smooth strongly convex losses and regularizers only (Lasso and other non-smooth penalties excluded), which removes many settings where universality questions are most actively studied (Thrampoulidis et al., Stojnic), and the 'systematic study of the reduced system' for the Gaussian-equivalence representations of Gerace et al./Dandi et al. is explicitly left to future work.

Presentation flaws: a LaTeX artifact ('lambda2') appears in the main covariance formula in Appendix D.3, and the footnote on page 5 referencing 'the submitted version' suggests an incompletely revised manuscript. Impact statement is perfunctory.

Given that the decisive novelty (a non-Gaussian comparison principle making the universality step explicit) is conjectural and the score characterization depends on an unavailable proof, the paper currently does not meet the bar of results that others can reliably build upon without first verifying the conjectures themselves.

strengths: Important and well-motivated question: the paper carefully distinguishes three notions of Gaussian universality (performance, score, minimizer) and provides a useful taxonomy of the literature (Table 1), clarifying exactly which prior works prove or assume which notion.

Honest framing: the authors explicitly flag the central comparison principle (Claim 4.1) as a conjecture and clearly state that Theorems 4.3, 4.4 and downstream results are conditional on it, rather than disguising conditionality.

The fixed-point system of Theorem 4.4 is clean and recovers known results as special cases: the classical ridge fixed-point equation (Section 5, with an RMT consistency check in Appendix D.2) and the Mai–Liao LFMM equations (Appendix F.1), which is a meaningful consistency check for the framework.

Theorem 7.1 (covariance-adjusted subspace confinement) is a crisp structural result with a clean Gaussian-integration-by-parts proof, and correctly identifies anisotropic noise covariance as the mechanism by which the asymptotic mean leaves the structured subspace.

Numerical evidence is well chosen to demonstrate the phenomenon: Figure 1 (elastic loss with bimodal features) shows performance universality holding at the squared-loss endpoint while breaking down elsewhere, and the MNIST experiment (Appendix G) demonstrates breakdown on realistic data; code is stated to be available.

Restricting attention to first two moments of the score, and proving the quadratic universality of smooth regularizers (Theorem 3.3) unconditionally under stated assumptions, is a genuinely useful technical ingredient.
weaknesses: The central technical engine of the paper is a conjecture. Claim 4.1 (the generalized CGMT for concentrated column designs) is unproven, and the headline results (Theorems 4.3, 4.4, and consequently 3.3's application, Corollary 5.1 beyond what is known from RMT, and the qualitative claims of Sections 6–7 that depend on them) are all conditional. The abstract and introduction say 'we show' and 'we derive' without consistently conveying that the min–max characterization rests on an unverified comparison principle; this materially weakens the paper's claim to settle when universality holds or breaks down.

Theorem 6.1 rests on Assumption 4 (minimizer universality), which is not proven here; the paper cites a proof as 'under preparation' in another preprint (Louart, 2026). Two of the four main contributions therefore depend on results that do not yet exist in the literature, which prevents readers from reliably building on the claims.

The assumptions are quite restrictive relative to the framing: smooth, twice-continuously differentiable, strongly convex losses and regularizers are required, explicitly excluding the Lasso and other non-smooth penalties that dominate the CGMT literature the paper positions itself against; Theorem 3.3 only controls the first two moments of the score.

Empirical validation is thin: the main experiment uses p = 30, n = 50, and the only other experiment is a single MNIST binary task. Given the conjectural theory, broader numerical support (larger dimensions, more losses/regularizers, systematic finite-size error analysis) would be needed to substantiate the claim that the conditional predictions are accurate.

There is substantial overlap with known breakdown phenomena: the failure of score universality when the estimator aligns with structured feature directions is already documented (Hu & Lu, 2022; Pesce et al., 2023; Mai & Liao, 2025). The novelty here is mainly an organizing framework and conditional characterization, so the marginal advance over existing literature is moderate.

Presentation flaws that inspire caution: the covariance deterministic equivalent on page 24 contains a raw-source typo ('sigma^2_epsilon + lambda2 theta*...'), and footnote 2 refers to 'the submitted version' and to a 2026 preprint, suggesting the manuscript was revised under time pressure and not carefully proofread; key stability assumptions for Theorem 4.3 (unique stable saddle point, local-uniform convergence, compact truncation) are invoked loosely and never verified even for the flagship ridge example.
Key dependencies on self-referential preprints (Louart, 2024; Louart, 2026) that a reader cannot verify reduce reproducibility of the conditional derivations.
